title: Kan-valued relative nerves are the classified left fibrations
statement:
Use the simplicial sets, horns, Kan spaces and ordinary nerves of [def-cbc-enhanced-diagrams-cones] and the left and cocartesian fibrations of [def-coef-infinity-fibrations]. Fix universes $\mathcal U\in\mathcal U'$. Let $C$ be a $\mathcal U$-small ordinary category and let $F:C\to\mathsf{sSet}_{\mathcal U}$ be a strict functor taking every object to a Kan complex. For a nonempty finite ordered set $J$, write $\Delta^J=N(J)$, viewing $J$ as an ordinary category; an order-preserving map $h:J\to K$ induces $\Delta(h):\Delta^J\to\Delta^K$ by postcomposition on the simplices of these nerves. Define $N_F(C)$ by the following data in dimension $r$: a functor $\sigma:[r]\to C$ and, for every nonempty subset $J\subseteq[r]$, a simplicial map $t_J:\Delta^J\to F(\sigma(\max J))$ satisfying
$$t_J|_{\Delta^I}=F(\sigma(\max I)\to\sigma(\max J))\circ t_I\qquad(\varnothing\ne I\subseteq J).$$
For $\theta:[s]\to[r]$, reindex $\sigma$ by $\theta$ and set $t'_J=t_{\theta(J)}\circ\Delta(\theta|_J)$ for nonempty $J\subseteq[s]$. Projection to $\sigma$ gives $p:N_F(C)\to N(C)$. Then $p$ is a left fibration, is also a cocartesian fibration, and every edge in its domain is $p$-cocartesian. The fiber over $c$ is naturally isomorphic to $F(c)$. Under these identifications cocartesian transport along $u:c\to d$ is the map $F(u)$, with its coherent composition data given by the strict functor $F$. Equivalently, using classification as defined in [lem-coef-space-valued-straightening], this is the left fibration classified by the coherent space-valued functor represented by $F$.

source.place: Definition 3.2.5.2; Remark 3.2.5.4; Corollary 3.2.5.19 (left fibrations) and Proposition 3.2.5.21 (cocartesian edges and classification). Read online; not archived in literature/. No Stacks tag states this infinity-categorical result.

proof.text: First check that the prescribed operators define a simplicial set. If $I\subseteq J$, the restriction of $t_{\theta(J)}\Delta(\theta|_J)$ to $\Delta^I$ equals $t_{\theta(J)}|_{\Delta^{\theta(I)}}\Delta(\theta|_I)$; the defining compatibility makes this $F(\sigma(\theta(\max I))\to\sigma(\theta(\max J)))t_{\theta(I)}\Delta(\theta|_I)$. Here monotonicity gives $\max\theta(I)=\theta(\max I)$, even for noninjective $\theta$. For another monotone $\eta$, image subsets satisfy $\theta(\eta(J))=(\theta\eta)(J)$ and the induced maps of nerves compose; hence applying the two reindexings equals reindexing by $\theta\eta$. Identity reindexing is the identity. Forgetting the $t_J$ commutes with these operators, so $p$ is simplicial.

source.place: Definition 3.2.5.2; Remark 3.2.5.4; Corollary 3.2.5.19; Proposition 3.2.5.21. Explicit direct argument by Q33, checked against these statements.

proof.text: Over the constant simplex at $c$, all transition maps are identities. The compatibility for $J\subseteq[r]$ therefore forces $t_J=t_{[r]}|_{\Delta^J}$. Conversely any simplex $x:\Delta^r\to F(c)$ supplies exactly these restrictions. The mutually inverse assignments $(\sigma,t)\mapsto t_{[r]}$ and $x\mapsto(\mathrm{const}_c,(x|_{\Delta^J})_J)$ commute with every monotone operator by step 1. They give a degreewise, hence simplicial, isomorphism $p^{-1}(c)\cong F(c)$, natural for maps of strict diagrams.

source.place: Definition 3.2.5.2; Remark 3.2.5.4; Corollary 3.2.5.19; Proposition 3.2.5.21. Explicit direct argument by Q33, checked against these statements.

proof.text: Consider a left horn lifting problem with $n\geq1$, $0\leq i<n$, and specified base simplex $\sigma:[n]\to C$. Put $V=[n]$, $A=V\setminus\{i\}$ and $K=F(\sigma(n))$. A nonempty subset $J\subseteq V$ occurs in the horn precisely when it omits some $k\ne i$. Consequently the horn determines compatible $t_J$ for all $J$ except $V$ and $A$. For each face $J_k=V\setminus\{k\}$, $k\ne i$, postcompose its given $t_{J_k}$ with $F(\sigma(\max J_k)\to\sigma(n))$. On an intersection indexed by nonempty $I\subseteq J_k\cap J_l$, both restrictions are $F(\sigma(\max I)\to\sigma(n))t_I$, by compatibility and strict composition in $F$. Thus these face maps glue to a map $a:\Lambda_i^n\to K$. Gluing here is degreewise: a simplex lies in a face precisely when its vertex image is contained in that face, and the two values agree on intersections.

source.place: Definition 3.2.5.2; Remark 3.2.5.4; Corollary 3.2.5.19; Proposition 3.2.5.21. Explicit direct argument by Q33, checked against these statements.

proof.text: Since $K$ is Kan, extend $a$ to $T:\Delta^n\to K$. Define the two missing data by $t_V=T$ and $t_A=T|_{\Delta^A}$; both have the correct target because $i<n$, so $\max A=n$. For a proper nonempty $I\subset A$, choose $k\in A\setminus I$. This $k\ne i$, so $I$ is contained in the known face $J_k$, and restricting $T$ to $I$ gives $F(\sigma(\max I)\to\sigma(n))t_I$. For any other known proper $J\subset V$, choose $k\ne i$ omitted by $J$ and use the same equality on $J$. These identities verify all compatibility equations involving either new datum; the old ones held in the horn. The resulting simplex of $N_F(C)$ lies over $\sigma$ and restricts to the prescribed horn. This includes $n=1,i=0$, where $A=\{1\}$ and the horn map is the prescribed initial vertex mapped into $F(\sigma(1))$. Thus $p$ has every left horn filler required in the definition.

source.place: Definition 3.2.5.2; Remark 3.2.5.4; Corollary 3.2.5.19; Proposition 3.2.5.21. Explicit direct argument by Q33, checked against these statements.

proof.text: The ordinary nerve $N(C)$ is a quasicategory directly from the nerve definition in [def-cbc-enhanced-diagrams-cones]. In dimension 2 the only inner horn specifies consecutive arrows $f_{01},f_{12}$; take $f_{02}=f_{12}f_{01}$. In dimension 3 either inner horn contains all edges and three triangular composition equations. For the missing triangle these equations and associativity give $f_{03}=f_{23}(f_{12}f_{01})=(f_{23}f_{12})f_{01}$, which is precisely its required equation. In dimensions $n\geq4$, every edge and triangle lies in a present face: its vertex set omits at least two vertices, so one can choose an omitted vertex distinct from the horn index. Thus the horn specifies all arrows $f_{ab}$ and the equations $f_{ac}=f_{bc}f_{ab}$. They define a functor $[n]\to C$ and its restriction is the given horn, since every face functor is determined by these arrows. These constructions fill every inner horn in $N(C)$. For $p$, any lifting problem against an inner horn already includes a base simplex; step 4 fills it because $0<i<n$ is within the left-horn range. To fill an inner horn in the total space $N_F(C)$, first fill its projected horn in $N(C)$ by the preceding argument, and then apply step 4. Hence $p$ is an inner fibration and $N_F(C)$ is a quasicategory.

source.place: Definition 3.2.5.2; Remark 3.2.5.4; Corollary 3.2.5.19; Proposition 3.2.5.21. Explicit direct argument by Q33, checked against these statements.

proof.text: For any edge $e$ of $N_F(C)$, every outer horn $\Lambda_0^n$, $n\geq2$, having $e$ as its $\{0,1\}$ edge is one of the lifting problems solved in step 4. The definition of a cocartesian edge therefore makes every edge $p$-cocartesian. Given $x$ over $c$ and $u:c\to d$, the $n=1,i=0$ case of step 4 supplies an edge with source $x$ over $u$. Since it is cocartesian and both source and base are quasicategories by step 5, the defining lift condition for a cocartesian fibration holds.

source.place: Definition 3.2.5.2; Remark 3.2.5.4; Corollary 3.2.5.19; Proposition 3.2.5.21. Explicit direct argument by Q33, checked against these statements.

proof.text:
Here is an explicit lift family, including its higher compatibilities. For a base simplex $\sigma:[r]\to C$, define $H_\sigma:F(\sigma(0))\times\Delta^r\to N_F(C)$ over $\sigma$. On an $m$-simplex $(x,b)$, where $x:\Delta^m\to F(\sigma(0))$ and $b:[m]\to[r]$, its base is $\sigma b$ and its subset datum is
$$t_J=F(\sigma(0)\to\sigma(b(\max J)))\,x|_{\Delta^J}.$$
The compatibility for nested subsets is exactly the composition law of $F$. Restriction along $\alpha:[q]\to[m]$ replaces $x$ by $x\Delta(\alpha)$ and $b$ by $b\alpha$, giving the same formula, so $H_\sigma$ is simplicial. On the vertex $j$ it is $F(\sigma(0)\to\sigma(j))$, using the fiber identification in step 2. In particular $H_u$ supplies, simultaneously for every simplex of $F(c)$, lifts from $x$ to $F(u)x$, whose vertexwise edges are cocartesian by step 6. For every monotone $\theta:[s]\to[r]$ the complete face-and-degeneracy identity is
$$H_\sigma(\mathrm{id}\times\Delta(\theta))=H_{\sigma\theta}(F(\sigma(0)\to\sigma(\theta(0)))\times\mathrm{id}).$$
Both sides have the same subset data because the two transition arrows compose to $\sigma(0)\to\sigma(\theta(b(\max J)))$. This establishes the coherence in all dimensions, including faces which remove the initial vertex. For $c\xrightarrow{u}d\xrightarrow{v}e$ the endpoint map is $F(vu)=F(v)F(u)$, and constant base simplices give the identity coherence. Thus the induced transport can be represented by the actual simplicial map $F(u)$ with the strict coherent composition data of $F$.

source.place: Definition 3.2.5.2; Remark 3.2.5.4; Corollary 3.2.5.19; Proposition 3.2.5.21. Explicit direct argument by Q33, checked against these statements.

proof.text: Use $A_\sigma,L_C,R_C$ and the classification convention in [lem-coef-space-valued-straightening]. For each base simplex $\sigma:[r]\to C$, a natural map $A_\sigma\to F$ is equivalent to a family of simplicial maps $t_J:\Delta^J\to F(\sigma(\max J))$: extract $t_J(z)$ by evaluating the summand $(J,z,\mathrm{id}_{\sigma(\max J)})$, and conversely send $(J,z,h)$ to $F(h)t_J(z)$. Naturality in $c$ forces this latter formula for every $h$. The quotient relation in $A_\sigma$ holds exactly when $t_J|_{\Delta^I}=F(\sigma(\max I)\to\sigma(\max J))t_I$. Thus the two assignments are inverse, including when any value is empty. The map $A_{\sigma\theta}\to A_\sigma$ induces on these families exactly $t'_J=t_{\theta(J)}\Delta(\theta|_J)$, including for noninjective $\theta$. A simplex of the right adjoint $R_CF$ over $\sigma$ is precisely a map from the object $(\Delta^r,\sigma)$ into $R_CF$; the adjunction identifies it with $\operatorname{Nat}(L_C(\Delta^r,\sigma),F)=\operatorname{Nat}(A_\sigma,F)$, since the identity simplex is terminal in the simplex category of $\Delta^r$. The preceding inverse assignments therefore give a simplicial isomorphism $E=N_F(C)\cong R_CF$ over $N(C)$, not a comparison using only transports or the coend of the $H_\sigma$. The total space $E$ is small: each degree uses a small set of base simplices and finitely many subsets, with all maps into small $F(c)$. Steps 4 and 5 give the small left fibration required by the comparison theorem. Since every $F(c)$ is Kan, that theorem's actual counit $L_C(R_CF)\to F$ is an objectwise weak homotopy equivalence; using the isomorphism just constructed yields $L_C(E)\to F$. Apply its straightening-comparison clause with $X=E$ and $D=F$. It follows that $\operatorname{St}_{N(C)}(p)\simeq N_{\mathrm{hc}}(F)$, which is exactly the classification clause. Step 7 continues to provide the separately asserted explicit cocartesian transport and composition data.
